title: What a Great Partnership Looks Like in Initial Teacher Training
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes sets out the features of a strong partnership between universities and schools in initial teacher training. Her central claim is that such a partnership should be a shared professional community, not a placement arrangement, so that trainees experience theory and practice as one coherent journey. She argues for shared responsibility across recruitment, mentoring, assessment and quality assurance, and for schools acting as genuine co-designers of the training curriculum. Mentoring is placed at the heart of the work, requiring protected time, training and status. She then addresses consistency with room for professional judgement, carefully chosen placements, honest handling of trainees who struggle, non-bureaucratic quality assurance and clear communication. The piece closes by insisting that pupils remain the final purpose and that a partnership is a designed bridge between the knowledge base of teaching and the reality of the classroom.
points: Hughes argues that universities and schools bring distinct expertise, research and curriculum structure on one side and the lived reality of classrooms on the other, and neither should be treated as secondary.
Schools should be co-designers of the training curriculum, so mentors know what trainees have been taught, what they are ready to practise and what comes next.
Mentoring must be treated as skilled professional practice with protected workload and regular development, not an add-on or a matter of knowing the lingo.
When a trainee struggles, she calls for a clear support plan naming the priority, the practice, the supporter and the review date rather than blame or panic.
Quality assurance should be a shared commitment to getting better, not one partner inspecting the other.
quotes: A great partnership in initial teacher training is more than an arrangement between a university and a school. At its best, it is a shared professional community with one clear purpose: to help new teachers learn how to improve the lives, learning and futures of the children and young people they teach.
When these two worlds work together well, trainees do not experience “theory” and “practice” as separate. They experience one coherent journey into the profession.
This means schools are not merely places where trainees “practise” what has been taught elsewhere. They are active contributors to the design and delivery of the training curriculum.

For this to happen, mentors need time, training and status. A strong partnership protects mentor workload, provides regular mentor development and treats mentoring as skilled professional practice, not as an add-on.
A great partnership is also honest about progression. Becoming a teacher is demanding. Trainees need encouragement, but they also need accurate feedback.

They use feedback to improve systems. They visit schools, moderate judgements and check that expectations are understood. Most importantly, they see quality assurance as a shared commitment to getting better, not as an inspection of one partner by another.
A great initial teacher training partnership, then, is not simply a placement system. It is a carefully designed bridge into the profession.
